title: The Only Habits of Great Leadership
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles synthesizes fifteen years leading schools into a pragmatic checklist of forty-two leadership principles spanning strategy, communication, curriculum, assessment, and operations. Emphasizing simplicity, iteration, visible metrics, and ruthless focus on the vital twenty percent, his framework prioritizes progress over style and insists that great leadership behavior, not trait, drives school improvement through deliberate systems and transparent accountability. Leaders who keep improvements to sixty-day cycles and measure impact through student progress optimize school culture and results. Walking and valuing people daily, explaining why decisions matter, and narrating what you see rather than what you think builds trust and buy-in. Standardizing repeated processes into checklists protects teacher time for what actually improves learning.
points: Leadership style makes no difference; what leaders do matters. Simple changes win adoption faster than complex ones because everyone can implement them.
Keep improvements to sixty-day cycles and measure impact through student progress grades; if a change doesn't measurably improve student outcomes, find why quickly.
Walk and value people daily, explain why decisions matter, and narrate what you see rather than what you think to build trust and buy-in.
Standardize repeated processes into checklists so anyone can execute them, delete non-essential tasks, and protect teacher time for what actually improves learning.
Test ideas in parallel classes for six weeks before rolling out; iterate constantly based on barriers encountered; data storytelling matters more than statistics alone.
quotes: There is no evidence that your leadership style makes any difference to the teams you lead. Instead, what matters is what leaders do.
Keep it simple. The simpler the change, the easier it is for everyone to implement.
If it is not in Rosenshine's Principles, The Learning and Forgetting Lab, Visible Learning, or the EEF Toolkit, ignore it unless it is covered there.
Find the 20% that makes the difference in every aspect of school life, and develop that. Be ruthless in minimising the 80% that make little difference.
People don't like numbers. Attach each statistic to a story so teachers understand why the numbers are important.” Archived from Dominic Salles School Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
